summary: Gives guidelines for designers of unicast applications that use UDP, with a main focus on congestion control, since UDP has none of its own. This is a Best Current Practice, and it was replaced by RFC 8085.

plainLanguage.summary: UDP is a simple way to send single messages, but it leaves three jobs to the program using it: slowing down when the path is crowded, coping with messages that are lost, duplicated or reordered, and securing the data. This RFC lists what application designers should do about each of them.

questions: how often should udp keep alives be sent
what is the safe udp message size
should i enable the udp checksum
how should a udp app handle loss and duplication
subtitle: What an application using UDP over IP should do about congestion, message size, reliability and middleboxes.

tldr.problem: UDP has no congestion control, no reliability and no protection from duplicated or reordered messages, so applications that use it must supply those properties themselves.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives rules for sending rate, for keeping datagrams under the path MTU, for handling loss and duplication, for getting past firewalls and NATs, and for protecting the data with a standard security protocol.
tldr.outcome: The rules became a Best Current Practice for unicast UDP applications. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 8085.

facts.label: Sending rate for low-volume applications
facts.value: At most one datagram per round-trip time

facts.label: Keep-alive interval
facts.value: Not more often than once every 15 seconds

today: RFC 5405 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 8085, so read that document for the current guidelines.

sections.title: Why UDP Needs Its Own Guidelines
sections.content:
The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) provides a minimal, unreliable, best-effort, message-passing transport to applications and upper-layer protocols. Compared to other transport protocols, UDP and its UDP-Lite variant are unique in that they do not establish end-to-end connections between communicating end systems. UDP communication consequently does not incur connection establishment and teardown overheads, and there is minimal associated end system state, so UDP can offer a very efficient communication transport to some applications.

A second unique characteristic of UDP is that it provides no inherent congestion control mechanisms. On many platforms, applications can send UDP datagrams at the line rate of the link interface, which is often much greater than the available path capacity, and doing so contributes to congestion along the path. The best current practice for congestion control in the Internet identifies two major reasons why congestion control is critical for the stable operation of the Internet: the prevention of congestion collapse, a state where an increase in network load results in a decrease in useful work done by the network, and the establishment of a degree of fairness, allowing multiple flows to share the capacity of a path reasonably equitably.

Because UDP itself provides no congestion control mechanisms, it is up to the applications that use UDP for Internet communication to employ suitable mechanisms to prevent congestion collapse and establish a degree of fairness. Congestion control is essential even at relatively slow transmission rates. An application that generates five 1500-byte UDP datagrams in one second can already exceed the capacity of a 56 Kb/s path.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP sends single messages without building a connection, and it has no built-in way to slow down when a path becomes crowded. That means the program using UDP has to do that job itself, or the network suffers.

sections.title: The Rules for Applications
sections.content:
Internet paths can have widely varying characteristics, including transmission delays, available bandwidths, congestion levels, reordering probabilities, supported message sizes, or loss rates, and the same path can have very different conditions over time. Applications that may be used on the Internet MUST NOT make assumptions about specific path characteristics. They MUST instead use mechanisms that let them operate safely under very different path conditions, which typically requires conservatively probing the current conditions of the path they communicate over to establish a transmission behavior that it can sustain and that is reasonably fair to other traffic sharing the path.

These mechanisms are difficult to implement correctly. For most applications, the use of one of the existing IETF transport protocols is the simplest method of acquiring them, so the RECOMMENDED alternative to the UDP usage described in the rest of the document is TCP, SCTP, SCTP-PR, or DCCP with its different congestion control types.

If used correctly, these more fully-featured transport protocols are not as heavy as is often claimed. The TCP algorithms have been continuously improved over decades and have reached a level of efficiency and correctness that custom application-layer mechanisms will struggle to duplicate. Many TCP implementations also allow connections to be tuned by an application, for example by disabling the Nagle algorithm, which improves communication latency at the expense of more frequent but still congestion-controlled transmissions, or by using the SYN cookie mechanism, which lets a server avoid maintaining per-connection state until the connection is established.
sections.plainLanguage: An application must not assume anything about the path it uses, because the path can change. Measuring the path and adapting is work that a ready-made transport protocol already does well, so using one is usually the simpler choice.

sections.title: Congestion Control for Different Kinds of Application
sections.content:
If an application or upper-layer protocol chooses not to use a congestion-controlled transport protocol, it SHOULD control the rate at which it sends UDP datagrams to a destination host. An application SHOULD perform congestion control over all UDP traffic it sends to a destination, independently from how it generates this traffic, so an application that forks multiple worker processes or otherwise uses multiple sockets SHOULD perform congestion control over the aggregate traffic.

For bulk transfer applications, those that exchange more than a small number of datagrams per round-trip time, the RFC says they SHOULD implement TCP-Friendly Rate Control, window-based TCP-like congestion control, or otherwise ensure compliance with the congestion control principles. Applications that choose neither TFRC nor TCP-like windowing SHOULD implement a scheme whose bandwidth use competes fairly with TCP within an order of magnitude.

For low data-volume applications, which at any time exchange only a small number of datagrams with a destination, those schemes bring little benefit because they only work over longer transmissions. Such applications SHOULD still control their transmission behavior by not sending on average more than one UDP datagram per round-trip time to a destination. They SHOULD maintain an estimate of the RTT, compute a smoothed RTT using the algorithm of RFC 2988, and back off their retransmission timer exponentially when a loss event occurs. An application that cannot maintain a reliable RTT estimate, either because it exchanges too few datagrams or because the destination sends no return traffic at all, SHOULD NOT send more than one datagram every 3 seconds, and SHOULD use an even less aggressive rate when possible. That 3-second interval was chosen from TCP's retransmission timeout when the RTT is unknown.

For UDP tunnels, the guidance depends on two factors: whether the payload traffic is IP-based, and whether the tunnel's UDP traffic volume corresponds to the payload volume. A tunnel carrying IP-based, congestion-controlled traffic SHOULD NOT employ its own congestion control, because congestion losses of the tunnelled traffic will already trigger a congestion response at the original senders. A tunnel carrying traffic that is not known to be IP-based, or is known to be IP-based but not congestion-controlled, SHOULD employ an appropriate congestion control mechanism. A tunnel that sends at a volume that does not correspond to the payload volume goes beyond the scope of these guidelines.
sections.plainLanguage: How much an application should send depends on what it is doing. A bulk transfer should behave like TCP. An application that only exchanges the occasional message should send about one message per round trip. A tunnel carrying ordinary IP traffic does not need its own control, because the traffic inside already has some.

sections.title: Message Size and Checksums
sections.content:
IP fragmentation lowers the efficiency and reliability of Internet communication: the loss of a single fragment results in the loss of an entire fragmented packet, because even if all other fragments are received correctly the original packet cannot be reassembled and delivered. Some network address translators and firewalls drop IP fragments, since translation only operates on complete IP packets and some firewall policies require inspection of complete packets. An application SHOULD NOT send UDP datagrams that result in IP packets that exceed the MTU of the path to the destination, and SHOULD either use the path MTU information provided by the IP layer or implement path MTU discovery itself.

Applications that do not follow the recommendation to do PMTU discovery SHOULD still avoid sending datagrams that would exceed the path MTU, and SHOULD fall back to sending messages shorter than the default effective MTU for sending. For IPv4, EMTU_S is the smaller of 576 bytes and the first-hop MTU; for IPv6, EMTU_S is 1280 bytes. To determine an appropriate UDP payload size, applications MUST subtract the size of the IP header and the length of the UDP header, which is 8 bytes, from the PMTU size.

The UDP header includes an optional 16-bit one's complement checksum, which provides a relatively weak integrity check and is not designed to detect physical-layer errors or malicious modification. Applications SHOULD enable UDP checksums, although RFC 768 permits the option to disable their use, and the use of the UDP checksum is REQUIRED when applications transmit UDP over IPv6. Applications that need stronger protection should add their own checks, for example a Cyclic Redundancy Check over the whole object being sent. A special class of application can use UDP-Lite, which changes the semantics of the payload length field into a checksum coverage length field so that a partly damaged payload is delivered rather than discarded, at the cost of checking only part of the data.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending a datagram larger than the path can carry means the packet gets split, and losing one piece loses the whole message. So find out how big the path can carry and stay under it. The UDP checksum is weak, so add your own check if the data matters.

sections.title: Reliability and Middleboxes
sections.content:
UDP does not retransmit lost packets, and applications that require reliable message delivery MUST implement an appropriate mechanism themselves. UDP also does not protect against datagram duplication, so an application may receive several copies of the same datagram and should handle that gracefully. The Internet can also delay some packets relative to others, causing reordering, so applications that require ordered delivery MUST reestablish ordering themselves. Delay spikes can be very large: TCP defines the Maximum Segment Lifetime as 2 minutes, and this document clarifies that the MSL value to be used for UDP SHOULD be the same 2 minutes, so applications SHOULD be robust to the reception of delayed or duplicate packets received within this interval.

Network address translators and firewalls are middleboxes that maintain per-flow state. Because UDP is connectionless, a middlebox creates that state when it sees a packet indicating a new flow and destroys it after a period during which no packets belonging to that flow have arrived, so return traffic that arrives after the state has timed out is dropped. Applications SHOULD be able to handle such communication failures and implement mechanisms to re-establish their sessions and state. Specialized applications, such as media transmissions, MAY send periodic keep-alive messages to refresh middlebox state, but keep-alives are NOT RECOMMENDED for general use, because they are unnecessary for many applications and can consume significant amounts of system and network resources. An application that needs them SHOULD NOT transmit them more frequently than once every 15 seconds, SHOULD use longer intervals when possible, and SHOULD apply slight random variations to their timing.

UDP also provides no flow control, and a UDP socket can receive packets from more than one source address, so applications that need to ensure they receive packets from a particular source address MUST implement the corresponding checks at the application layer or explicitly request that the operating system filter the received packets.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP can lose, duplicate and reorder messages, and the application has to cope. Routers and firewalls in the middle also forget a UDP conversation after a while, so an application may have to start it again, sometimes by sending an occasional keep-alive.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
UDP does not provide communications security. Applications that need to protect their communications against eavesdropping, tampering, or message forgery SHOULD employ end-to-end security services provided by other IETF protocols. Applications that respond to short requests with potentially large responses are vulnerable to amplification attacks, and SHOULD authenticate the sender before responding. The source IP address of a request is not a useful authenticator, because it can be spoofed.

One option is IPsec, which can authenticate flows of IP packets through the Authentication Header and encrypt and authenticate through the Encapsulating Security Payload, and which applications configure with the Internet Key Exchange. If an application only requires authentication, ESP with no encryption but with authentication is often a better option than AH, because ESP can operate across middleboxes. A second option is Datagram Transport Layer Security, which provides communication privacy by encrypting UDP payloads but does not protect the UDP headers, and which applications can implement without relying on operating system support. Other options include the GSS-API security framework, Cryptographic Message Syntax, the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol for securing RTP sessions over UDP, and S/MIME or OpenPGP for protecting larger stand-alone objects such as files or messages.

Like congestion control mechanisms, security mechanisms are difficult to design and implement correctly, so it is RECOMMENDED that applications employ well-known standard security mechanisms such as DTLS or IPsec rather than inventing their own.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP encrypts nothing by itself. If the data matters, use a standard security protocol such as DTLS or IPsec. Also, do not answer a short request with a huge reply without checking who asked, because that lets others use your machine to attack someone else.

viz.caption: THE THREE KINDS OF APPLICATION AND THEIR SENDING RULES (RFC 5405)

items.title: Bulk transfer
items.text: More than a small number of datagrams per round trip. Use TFRC, TCP-like windowing, or a scheme that competes fairly with TCP within an order of magnitude.

items.title: Low data volume
items.text: Only a small number of datagrams with a destination. Send no more than one datagram per round-trip time on average, and back off on loss.

items.title: No return traffic
items.text: The destination never sends anything back, so loss cannot be detected. Send at most one datagram every 3 seconds.

items.title: Tunnel carrying IP traffic
items.text: If the tunnelled traffic is IP-based and congestion-controlled, the tunnel should not add its own congestion control.
